1934年（昭和9年）創業の老舗喫茶。芝居の世界に憧れた初代・原田邦雄が、東京の: An old coffee shop founded in 1934 (Showa 9). The first owner, who longed for the world of theatre, is said to have named it after the Tokyo avant-garde company 'Tsukiji Shogekijo'. The first owner, who had never studied architecture, created the space by conveying ideas to craftsmen by instinct: plaster walls, colourful irregular tiles, carving on pillars and skirting boards, oil paintings and wood-carved reliefs, decorative plates, clocks and other heavy furnishings, giving the air of having wandered into an old European castle. The 2nd floor was originally living quarters, but was converted into part of the shop around 1951–52. Handed down over three generations since its founding, it is now kept by the third generation. One of the oldest surviving coffee shops in the city, going back to the 1930s when Kyoto's coffee culture began.

Ichikawaya Coffee is a coffee shop opened in 2015 in the Higashiyama, Kyoto neighbourhood where Kiyomizu-yaki kilns once gathered. The building was the Kiyomizu-yaki workshop and home of owner Yosuke Ichikawa's grandfather, where Ichikawa also lived. This roughly 200-year-old Kyoto townhouse once faced demolition, but out of the wish 'to keep this place', Ichikawa decided on a full renovation costing about four times a new build. Rebuilt by the Kyoto townhouse builders (京町家作事組), it was reborn as a large townhouse café looking onto a courtyard garden. In the Ichikawa family, both the grandfather and father were Kiyomizu-yaki potters, and the elder brother has also followed the path of ceramics. Only Ichikawa loved coffee, enough to roast as a hobby from student days, and after 18 years of training at the famous Inoda Coffee went independent and opened this shop.

The signature is the 'seasonal fruit sandwich': seasonal fruit that changes each month, between fluffy white bread and rich fresh cream. Carefully made, from choosing and cutting the fruit to the sweetness of the cream, it's so popular that a queue forms before opening. The coffee is roasted in-house daily on the shop's roaster and slowly brewed by flannel drip. There are three blends — Ichikawaya Blend, Seiji (celadon) Blend and Umamachi Blend — each served in Kiyomizu-yaki cups made by the father or brother. Even the cups are designed for each blend: the Ichikawaya Blend cup has a thin rim and thick base for ease of drinking and heat retention, and the Seiji Blend cup a wide mouth to lift the aroma. There are also items such as an egg sandwich and demi-glace omurice.
